title: Redirection, pipes & xargs
about: Standard input, output and error; redirecting to and from files; the order of redirections; here-documents; pipes and their exit status; tee, xargs and command substitution as ways of connecting programs.

questions.title: The three standard streams
questions.text: Match each stream with its file descriptor and usual connection.

pairs.r: Descriptor 0, normally the keyboard
pairs.why: Where a program reads its input.

pairs.r: Descriptor 1, normally the screen
Descriptor 2, normally the screen

extras.why: Descriptors above 2 are free for your own use.

questions.title: Why two output streams
questions.text: Why do programs have separate output streams for normal results and for errors?

options.t: So that errors remain visible (or can be logged elsewhere) even when the normal output is redirected to a file or another program.
options.why: The two can be redirected independently.

options.t: Because the screen can only show one at a time.
Because errors are sent to another computer.
Because the kernel counts them separately for billing.

questions.title: Only stdout redirected
questions.text: What do you see on the screen after `ls f nonexistent > out.txt` when `f` exists and `nonexistent` does not?

options.t: The error message about `nonexistent`; the line `f` went into `out.txt`.
options.why: `>` redirects only stdout; stderr still goes to the terminal.

options.t: Nothing, both streams went into the file.

options.why: The listing went to the file.

questions.title: Which stream
questions.text: Through which stream does each message usually appear?

items.t: The list of files printed by `ls`
items.why: The normal result of the command.
Its purpose is to write output.

items.t: `ls: cannot access 'x': No such file or directory`

items.why: An error reported by the shell.

questions.title: Output redirection operators
questions.text: Match each operator with its effect.

pairs.r: Send stdout to `file`, replacing its contents
Append stdout to the end of `file`
Send stderr to `file`
Send both stdout and stderr to `file`
Discard stdout
pairs.why: The special file that swallows everything.

questions.title: Overwrite or append
questions.text: `echo one > t; echo two > t; echo three >> t; cat t` prints which lines?

questions.title: Truncation happens first
questions.text: What is left in the file after `cat data > data`?

options.t: An empty file: the shell truncates `data` when setting up the redirection, before `cat` starts reading it.
options.why: Never redirect a command's output onto its own input.

options.t: An unchanged file with the same contents.
An error prevents the command from running.
options.why: GNU `cat` refuses in some cases, but the plain shell would already have emptied the file.

questions.title: Sort in place
questions.text: Why does `sort names > names` not sort the file `names`?

options.t: The redirection empties `names` before `sort` reads it, so `sort` sorts nothing.
options.why: Use `sort names -o names`, or write to a temporary file and move it back.

questions.title: Sort into the same file
questions.text: Sort the file `names` and write the result back into it, safely: `sort names {{0}} names`
questions.note: `-o` lets `sort` finish reading before it writes the output file.

wrong.why: That truncates the input first, as seen above.
A pipe needs a command on the right-hand side.

questions.title: Redirection before execution
questions.text: What happens when you run `nonexistent_cmd > out.txt 2>/dev/null` and the command does not exist?

options.t: `out.txt` is still created (empty), because the shell opens the redirections before it tries to start the command.
Nothing is created, since the command never ran.
options.why: The redirections were set up first.

options.t: The shell stops with a syntax error.

questions.title: Several redirections of the same stream
questions.text: What does `echo hi > o > p` do?

options.t: Both files are created (or truncated), but the text is written only to `p`, the last one.
options.why: Each redirection replaces the previous one for that descriptor.

options.t: The text is written to both files.
The text is written to `o` only.

questions.title: Protect against overwrite
questions.text: Which shell setting makes `>` refuse to overwrite an existing file, and which operator forces it anyway?

options.why: `-e` makes the shell exit on errors.

questions.title: Discard errors
questions.text: Run `ls /root` but hide the error messages: `ls /root {{0}}`

wrong.why: That discards the normal output, not the errors.
Same: stream 1 is the normal output.

questions.title: Null and zero
questions.text: What happens to data written to `/dev/null`?

options.t: It is discarded, and the write always succeeds.
options.why: Reading from it returns end-of-file immediately.

options.t: It is stored in a hidden file.
It is sent to the printer.

questions.title: Both to a file
questions.text: Which command sends both the normal output and the errors of `ls f nonexist` to `out.txt`?

options.why: First stdout goes to the file; then stderr is pointed at where stdout currently goes.
Stderr is pointed at the terminal (stdout's old place) before stdout moves to the file.
Only the errors go to the file.
That sends stdout to the stderr destination, which is the terminal.

questions.title: The wrong order
questions.text: What does `ls f nonexist 2>&1 > out.txt` do?

options.t: The error message stays on the terminal and only the normal output goes to `out.txt`.
options.why: Redirections are processed left to right; `2>&1` copied the old destination of stdout, the terminal.

options.t: Both streams go to the file.
Both streams stay on the screen.

questions.title: Copy, not link
questions.text: What does `2>&1` mean precisely?

options.t: Make descriptor 2 a duplicate of descriptor 1, pointing wherever stdout points **at that moment**.
options.why: It copies the current destination; it does not create a permanent link.

options.t: Send the text "2" to the file named "1".

options.why: Nothing is duplicated except the descriptor.

questions.title: Errors through a pipe
questions.text: What does `ls f nonexist 2>&1 | wc -l` count?

options.t: Both the normal and the error lines, because stderr is now joined to the pipe: 2 lines.
options.why: Without `2>&1` only stdout would enter the pipe.

options.t: Nothing, since pipes carry no errors.

questions.title: Only errors through the pipe
questions.text: What does `ls f nonexist 2>&1 >/dev/null | wc -l` print?

options.why: stderr goes to the pipe (old stdout), then stdout is discarded: only the error line is counted.
The error line enters the pipe.
There are only two lines of output.

questions.title: Build the redirection
questions.text: Put the parts in order to run `make`, keeping all its output (normal and error) in `build.log` and showing nothing on screen.

items.why: Point stdout at the file first.
Then make stderr follow stdout to the file; the terminal stays quiet.

questions.title: Results of the order
questions.text: Match each command with where `ls f nonexist` output ends up (`f` exists, `nonexist` does not).

pairs.r: Both lines in the file `o`
The error on the screen, the `f` line in the file
pairs.why: stderr copied the terminal, stdout moved.

pairs.r: The same result as the first form, written with the bash shorthand
`f` on the screen, the error in the file

extras.r: Both lines on the screen and an empty file
extras.why: None of the forms does that.

questions.title: Input operators
questions.text: Match each form with its meaning.

pairs.r: Read the standard input of `cmd` from `file`
Take the following lines up to `EOF` as input (here-document)
Use the string plus a newline as input (here-string)
A here-document without any expansion inside

questions.title: Redirection versus argument
questions.text: What is the difference between `wc -l data.txt` and `wc -l < data.txt`?

options.t: The first gives `wc` the file name and prints it in the result; in the second the shell opens the file and `wc` just reads its stdin, so no name is shown.
options.why: Useful when you need only the number.

options.t: The first reads from the keyboard.
They fail if the file has more than one line.

questions.title: Unquoted here-document
questions.text: What does `cat <<EOF` print for a body line `home: $HOME`?

options.why: With an unquoted delimiter the shell expands variables and substitutions in the body.

questions.title: Quoted delimiter
questions.text: How does `cat <<'EOF'` differ from `cat <<EOF`?

options.t: With the delimiter quoted, nothing in the body is expanded: `$HOME` and `$(cmd)` stay as typed.
It stops at the first blank line.
options.why: The delimiter is what ends it.

options.t: It appends the text to a file.

questions.title: Tabs in here-documents
questions.text: What does the `-` in `<<-EOF` do?

options.t: It strips leading tab characters from the body lines and from the delimiter line, so you can indent the here-document in a script.
options.why: It strips tabs only, not spaces.

options.t: It strips all leading spaces and tabs.

questions.title: Here-string
questions.text: What does `wc -w <<< "one two three"` print?

options.why: The string becomes the input of `wc`.
That is the number of characters.
That would be the line count.

questions.title: Uppercase a string
questions.text: Turn a literal string into upper case without a pipe: `tr a-z A-Z {{0}} "hello"`
questions.note: `echo hello | tr a-z A-Z` is the pipe alternative.

wrong.why: That would read from a file called `hello`.
A pipe needs a command on its left.

questions.title: Two inputs
questions.text: Which command gives `sort` its input from the file `u` and writes the result to `v`?

options.why: Both redirections can be combined in any order.
The last operator is missing its file.
That reads from `v` and overwrites `u`, the opposite of the goal.
A pipe needs a command on the right.

questions.title: What a pipe does
questions.text: What does `cmd1 | cmd2` do?

options.t: It connects the standard output of `cmd1` to the standard input of `cmd2`, and runs both at the same time.
It runs `cmd1`, waits, and then runs `cmd2` with the saved output.
It writes the output of `cmd1` into a file called `cmd2`.
It passes the exit status of `cmd1` as an argument to `cmd2`.
options.why: Only data flows through the pipe.

questions.title: Pipe versus redirection
questions.text: What is the difference between `cmd > file` and `cmd | other`?

options.t: `>` connects a program to a **file**, while `|` connects two **programs**.
options.why: A common mistake is writing `cmd > other`, which creates a file named `other`.
It works at the prompt too.

questions.title: Pipe and errors
questions.text: In `ls nonexistent | wc -l`, what is counted and what shows on the screen?

options.t: `wc` counts 0 lines; the error message still appears on the terminal, because a pipe carries only stdout.

questions.title: Exit status of a pipeline
questions.text: What is `$?` after `false | true` in bash (default options)?

options.t: `0`, the status of the last command of the pipeline.
options.why: Use `${PIPESTATUS[@]}` or `set -o pipefail` to notice the failure.

options.t: `1`, the status of the first command.
`1` because any failure marks the pipeline as failed.

questions.title: pipefail
questions.text: What does `set -o pipefail` change?

options.t: A pipeline returns the status of the last command that failed, instead of only the last command's status.
options.why: Helpful in scripts to notice that an early stage failed.

options.t: It stops pipelines from ever failing.
It sends errors through the pipe.

questions.title: Useless use of cat
questions.text: What is the preferred way of writing `cat file | grep root`?

options.why: `grep` can read the file itself: one process fewer.
`cat` would try to open files named `grep` and `root`.

questions.title: A classic pipeline
questions.text: Put the stages of "how many different shells are used in `/etc/passwd`?" in order.

items.why: Extract the shell field from each line.
Collapse each group to one line.

questions.title: Left to right
questions.text: Why does `sort | head file` not do what `sort file | head` does?

options.t: In the first, `sort` has no file and reads the keyboard, while `head` reads `file` and ignores the pipe.
options.why: The file operand must go to the command that should read it.

questions.title: Pipe to both
questions.text: How can you both save the output of a command in a file and pass it on to the next command?

options.why: `tee` copies its input to a file and to its output.
Redirecting stdout leaves nothing for the pipe.
That writes into a file named `next`.

questions.title: xargs idea
questions.text: Why does `find . -name '*.tmp' | xargs rm` need `xargs`, instead of just `find ... | rm`?

options.t: `rm` takes file names as **arguments** and ignores its standard input; `xargs` turns lines of input into arguments.
`rm` does not support pipes at all.
options.why: It is a matter of arguments, not of pipes.

questions.title: xargs options
questions.text: Match each option with its effect.

pairs.r: Pass one argument per command invocation
pairs.why: Runs the command once per item.

pairs.r: Insert each input item where `{}` appears in the command
pairs.why: Also implies one invocation per line.

pairs.r: Input items are separated by NUL characters
Do not run the command when the input is empty
Run up to four commands in parallel

questions.title: Names with spaces
questions.text: Why is `find . -print0 | xargs -0 rm` safer than `find . | xargs rm`?

options.t: File names can contain spaces or newlines; NUL separators cannot appear in names, so nothing is split wrongly.
options.why: Otherwise `a b` would be treated as two files.

options.t: `-0` limits the deletion to empty files.
options.why: It has nothing to do with that.
It prints names with NUL separators.

questions.title: xargs with nothing
questions.text: What does `printf '' | xargs echo empty` print with GNU `xargs`?

options.why: GNU `xargs` runs the command once even with no input, unless `-r` is given.

options.t: Nothing, since there is no input.

options.why: The command is run with the given text.

questions.title: Batching
questions.text:
What does `printf 'a
b
c
' | xargs -n2 echo` print?

options.why: The items are grouped two at a time.
`-n2` limits each call to two arguments.
Grouping starts with the first items.

questions.title: Substitution instead of xargs
questions.text: What is one risk of `rm $(find . -name '*.tmp')` compared with `find ... -delete`?

options.t: The shell splits the output on spaces and newlines, so file names with spaces break, and a very long list may exceed the argument limit.
It deletes files that do not match.
options.why: It deletes exactly the names printed, possibly mangled.

questions.title: Copy with find
questions.text: Which command copies all `.sh` files below `~` into `temporal` using `xargs`?

options.why: The names would be added after `temporal/`, copying into wrong places.
Writes the list into a file called `cp`.

questions.title: Pipes, substitution or xargs
questions.text: Which tool do you use to put the output of a command **inside** another command's argument list, as in `echo Hello $(whoami)`?

options.why: A pipe feeds standard input, not arguments.

questions.title: exec redirection
questions.text: What does `exec 2> err.log` do in a script?

options.t: From then on, the standard error of the script and all commands it runs goes to `err.log`.
options.why: `exec` with only redirections changes the shell's own descriptors.

options.t: It redirects only the next command.

questions.title: Custom descriptors
questions.text: Match each `exec` form with its effect.

pairs.r: Open `file` for reading as descriptor 3
Open `file` for writing as descriptor 3
Make descriptor 4 a copy of descriptor 3
Close descriptor 3

questions.title: Write to stderr in a script
questions.text: Which line makes a script print an error message on standard error?

options.why: Redirect the stdout of `echo` to descriptor 2.

questions.title: Logging in cron
questions.text: A script is run by `cron` and you want everything it prints (both streams) appended to `/var/log/job.log`. Which redirection do you add?

options.why: Append stdout, then send stderr to the same place.
The wrong order: stderr would not follow the file.
It overwrites the log on each run and loses the errors.
The right side of a pipe must be a command.

questions.title: Swap streams
questions.text: What does `{ echo out; echo err >&2; } >/dev/null` show on the terminal?

options.why: Only stdout was discarded; the message sent to stderr is still visible.

questions.title: Read input in a loop
questions.text: What is wrong with `cat names | while read n; do ...; done` if the loop must change a variable for later use?

options.t: The loop runs in a subshell because of the pipe, so assignments made inside are lost when it ends; use `while read n; do ...; done < names`.
options.why: Redirection keeps the loop in the current shell.
It ends at end of input.

questions.title: Which redirection
questions.text: You want the results of `ls` in `list.txt`, **adding** them to what is already there. Which command?
